## Keep or rush

In class order, as on the class slides. Planned total 78 of the 80 minutes.

| Item | Min | | If short |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Discussion 1: Absurd Trolley Problems, and which framework each side of a disagreement used | 10 | Rush | Play for four minutes; one disagreement from the room |
| Discussion 2 (the slides' activity 1): what the Belmont--Menlo principles and the five Cs require of a model that decides about people; groups describe theirs | 14 | Rush | Show the GP example; each group adds one requirement for its own scenario; two groups report |
| Problem 1: a safety course for riders, four variables and the adjustment formula, with feedback | 13 | Keep | Work (b) and (c) together; say (d): the course went to the riders most likely to have an accident, and adjusting for $Z$ alone leaves the night-work back door open |
| Break | 5 | Keep | |
| Problem 2: backdoor paths in three graphs, with feedback | 12 | Keep | Graphs 1 and 2, and (c): adjusting for $C$ opens the path |
| Discussion 3 (the slides' activity 2): three groups make the case for one framework, then the vote | 23 | Keep | Eight minutes to prepare, one minute each, then the vote |
| The task for next time | 1 | Keep | Read the task aloud |

: {tbl-colwidths="[32,6,16,46]"}

Minimum class, about 45 minutes: problems 1 and 2, the break, discussion 3 in its short form and the task for next time. With more time, add discussion 2 back first.

## If you read on

How it runs

- The order and the timings follow the class slides, including the five-minute break between the problems. Open the [complete class sheet](https://ethics4ds.com/teachers/wk03/class_complete.html) on screen: green boxes are hints, opened in order after a few minutes; blue boxes are answers and example answers.
- Discussion 1 needs one phone or laptop per group for [Absurd Trolley Problems](https://neal.fun/absurd-trolley-problems/). Groups will not finish the game; stop them at six minutes.
- Discussion 2: every group takes both the Belmont--Menlo principles and the five Cs. The slides' GP example is the first blue box; the second, on checking benefit claims, is for after the groups have reported.
- Problem 1 writes the treatment $T$; the lecture and the notes write $X$. All four variables enter the calculation: the adjustment set is $\{Z, W\}$, and the formula averages over the four groups of riders. The difference changes sign after adjustment.
- Problem 2 goes past the lecture, which defined blocking for forks and chains only. The sheet states the rule for colliders, from the reading. Collider stratification is a core item of week 5; this is where students first meet it.
- Discussion 3: three groups, with the slides' three statements (the lecture also covered pragmatic ethics, which is not one of them). Fifteen minutes to prepare, two minutes each, then the vote. Everyone votes for the account they find most convincing, which need not be the one they argued for.
- Everything headed "Optional, can be done at home" is outside the class, including the R simulation (coding C).

What students should see

- Problem 1: $\{Z, W\}$; 0.12 against 0.09 observed, so riders who took the course had an accident rate 3 points higher; 0.07 against 0.12 adjusted, an effect of $-0.05$. For (d): the 300 riders who took the course would have had about 57 accidents without it, against 36; adjusting for $Z$ alone gives about $-0.025$, because $T \leftarrow W \to Y$ stays open.
- Problem 2: graph 1, $\{A\}$ or $\{B\}$; graph 2, the empty set, and adjusting for $C$ opens $T \leftarrow A \to C \leftarrow B \to Y$; graph 3, four backdoor paths and $\{A, C\}$ or $\{B, C\}$; with only $C$ measured, no set works.
- Discussion 2: requirements stated as mechanisms (an opt-out, an audit by group, a data-retention rule), and the distinction between accuracy and the effect of using the model.

Where they get stuck

- Problem 1(c): weighting each group by its share of the riders who took the course, which gives back 0.12, instead of its share of all riders.
- Problem 1(a): adjusting for $Z$ only, because $Z \to W$ seems to cover $W$. The path $T \leftarrow W \to Y$ does not pass through $Z$.
- Calling the 3 points of problem 1(b) "biased" without saying of what. As a description of riders who took the course against the others, it is correct; as an estimate of the effect it is biased.
- Problem 2(a): counting $T \to Y$, or a path that leaves $T$ along an arrow out of it, as a backdoor path.
- Problem 2(b), graph 3: stopping at $\{C\}$.
- Problem 2(c): assuming that a variable measured before $T$ is always safe to adjust for.
- Discussion 3: groups that attack the other frameworks instead of making the case for their own. Ask for their best case first.
